claim: Human plasma contains > 40,000 different coding and non-coding RNAs that are potential biomarkers for human diseases.
source: Human plasma contains > 40,000 different coding and non-coding RNAs that are potential biomarkers for human diseases.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by the comprehensive TGIRT-seq analysis presented in the manuscript, which detected RNAs from >19,000 protein-coding genes plus numerous non-coding RNA species.

claim: TGIRT-seq combined with peak calling was used to simultaneously profile all RNA biotypes in apheresis-prepared human plasma pooled from healthy individuals.
source: Here, we used thermostable group II intron reverse transcriptase sequencing (TGIRT-seq) combined with peak calling to simultaneously profile all RNA biotypes in apheresis-prepared human plasma pooled from healthy individuals.
evidence: This is a methodological claim directly stated in the abstract describing the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Human plasma contains largely fragmented mRNAs from > 19,000 protein-coding genes.
source: Extending previous TGIRT-seq analysis, we found that human plasma contains largely fragmented mRNAs from > 19,000 protein-coding genes, abundant full-length, mature tRNAs and other structured small non-coding RNAs, and less abundant tRNA fragments and mature and pre-miRNAs.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in Figure 3 and related text showing detection of mRNAs from 15,000 to 19,000 different protein-coding genes.

claim: Human plasma contains abundant full-length, mature tRNAs and other structured small non-coding RNAs.
source: Extending previous TGIRT-seq analysis, we found that human plasma contains largely fragmented mRNAs from > 19,000 protein-coding genes, abundant full-length, mature tRNAs and other structured small non-coding RNAs, and less abundant tRNA fragments and mature and pre-miRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1C-D showing that tRNAs are the most abundant class of sncRNAs in plasma, and Figure 1—figure supplements 3-5 showing full-length mature tRNAs and other structured sncRNAs.

claim: Many of the mRNA fragments identified by peak calling correspond to annotated protein-binding sites.
source: Many of the mRNA fragments identified by peak calling correspond to annotated protein-binding sites and/or have stable predicted secondary structures that could afford protection from plasma nucleases.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4 showing that 467 peaks (50.7%) contained or overlapped an ENCODE eCLIP annotated RBP-binding site, and Figure 5 showing examples of such peaks.

claim: Many of the mRNA fragments identified by peak calling have stable predicted secondary structures that could afford protection from plasma nucleases.
source: Many of the mRNA fragments identified by peak calling correspond to annotated protein-binding sites and/or have stable predicted secondary structures that could afford protection from plasma nucleases.
evidence: This is supported by RNAfold analysis showing that 213 of 221 exon and pseudogene peaks could be folded into stable RNA secondary structures with ΔG ≤ −12 kcal/mol, and simulations showing this enrichment was statistically significant (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).

claim: Peak calling identified novel repeat RNAs, miRNA-sized RNAs, and putatively structured intron RNAs of potential biological, evolutionary, and biomarker significance.
source: Peak calling also identified novel repeat RNAs, miRNA-sized RNAs, and putatively structured intron RNAs of potential biological, evolutionary, and biomarker significance, including a family of full-length excised intron RNAs, subsets of which correspond to mirtron pre-miRNAs or agotrons.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 8-13 showing various types of repeat RNAs, short RNAs, and intron RNAs identified by peak calling.

claim: Peak calling identified a family of full-length excised intron RNAs, subsets of which correspond to mirtron pre-miRNAs or agotrons.
source: Peak calling also identified novel repeat RNAs, miRNA-sized RNAs, and putatively structured intron RNAs of potential biological, evolutionary, and biomarker significance, including a family of full-length excised intron RNAs, subsets of which correspond to mirtron pre-miRNAs or agotrons.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 9 showing examples of full-length excised intron RNAs, and Figure 4F showing that 13 corresponded to annotated agotrons and 10 to annotated mirtrons.

claim: Extracellular RNAs in human plasma have been avidly pursued as potential biomarkers for cancer and other human diseases.
source: Extracellular RNAs in human plasma have been avidly pursued as potential biomarkers for cancer and other human diseases (Schwarzenbach et al., 2011; Akat et al., 2014; Rapisuwon et al., 2016; Tsang et al., 2017; Cheung et al., 2019; Pardini et al., 2019; Sole et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a background claim supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: In healthy individuals, plasma RNAs arise largely by cell death or secretion from cells in blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes, and liver.
source: In healthy individuals, plasma RNAs arise largely by cell death or secretion from cells in blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes, and liver, while in cancer and other diseases, plasma RNAs may arise by necrosis or secretion from tumors or other damaged tissues, potentially providing diagnostic information (Lo et al., 1999; Turchinovich et al., 2011; Koh et al., 2014; Kishikawa et al., 2015; Kishikawa et al., 2016; Akat et al., 2019; Giraldez et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a background claim supported by citations and is consistent with the tissue-of-origin analysis presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Plasma contains active RNases.
source: As plasma contains active RNases (Kamm and Smith, 1972; Tsui et al., 2002), the extracellular RNAs that persist there are thought to be protected from degradation by bound proteins, RNA structure, or encapsulation in extracellular vesicles (EVs).
evidence: This is a background claim supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Extracellular RNAs that persist in plasma are thought to be protected from degradation by bound proteins, RNA structure, or encapsulation in extracellular vesicles (EVs).
source: As plasma contains active RNases (Kamm and Smith, 1972; Tsui et al., 2002), the extracellular RNAs that persist there are thought to be protected from degradation by bound proteins, RNA structure, or encapsulation in extracellular vesicles (EVs).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the introduction and supported by the findings of the study showing enrichment of RBP-binding sites and stable RNA structures in called peaks.

claim: Retroviral RTs have inherently low fidelity and processivity.
source: Retroviral RTs have inherently low fidelity and processivity and even those that are highly engineered have difficulty reverse transcribing through stable RNA secondary structures or post-transcriptional modifications, resulting in under-representation of 5'-RNA sequences and aborted reads that can be mistaken for RNA fragments (Nottingham et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a background claim about the limitations of retroviral RTs supported by citation.

claim: TGIRT enzymes have high fidelity, processivity, and strand-displacement activity.
source: In addition to high fidelity, processivity, and strand-displacement activity, group II intron RTs have a proficient template-switching activity that enables efficient, seamless attachment of RNA-seq adapter sequences to target RNAs without RNA tailing or ligation (Mohr et al., 2013; Lentzsch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a background claim about TGIRT enzyme properties supported by citations.

claim: Group II intron RTs have a proficient template-switching activity that enables efficient, seamless attachment of RNA-seq adapter sequences to target RNAs without RNA tailing or ligation.
source: In addition to high fidelity, processivity, and strand-displacement activity, group II intron RTs have a proficient template-switching activity that enables efficient, seamless attachment of RNA-seq adapter sequences to target RNAs without RNA tailing or ligation (Mohr et al., 2013; Lentzsch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a background claim about TGIRT enzyme properties supported by citations and utilized in the TGIRT-seq method shown in Figure 1A.

claim: TGIRT enzymes pause at post-transcriptional modifications but eventually read through by characteristic patterns of mis-incorporation that can be used to identify the modification.
source: Further, unlike retroviral RTs, which tend to dissociate from RNAs at post-transcriptional modifications that affect base pairing, TGIRT enzymes pause at such modifications but eventually read through by characteristic patterns of mis-incorporation that can be used to identify the modification (Katibah et al., 2014; Nottingham et al., 2016; Qin et al., 2016; Li et al., 2017; Safra et al., 2017; Shurtleff et al., 2017; Zubradt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a background claim about TGIRT enzyme properties supported by multiple citations and demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplements 3-4 showing misincorporation at known modification sites.

claim: TGIRT-seq gives relatively uniform 5'- and 3'-sequence coverage of mRNAs when initiating conventionally from an annealed oligo(dT) primer.
source: This combination of activities enables TGIRT enzymes to give relatively uniform 5'- and 3'-sequence coverage of mRNAs when initiating conventionally from an annealed oligo(dT) primer (Mohr et al., 2013) and to give full-length, end-to-end reads of tRNAs and other structured small ncRNAs, when initiating by template switching to the 3' end of the RNA (Mohr et al., 2013; Katibah et al., 2014; Nottingham et al., 2016; Qin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a background claim supported by citations and demonstrated in Figure 3F showing uniform coverage for TGIRT-seq compared to SMART-Seq.

claim: TGIRT-seq gives full-length, end-to-end reads of tRNAs and other structured small ncRNAs when initiating by template switching to the 3' end of the RNA.
source: This combination of activities enables TGIRT enzymes to give relatively uniform 5'- and 3'-sequence coverage of mRNAs when initiating conventionally from an annealed oligo(dT) primer (Mohr et al., 2013) and to give full-length, end-to-end reads of tRNAs and other structured small ncRNAs, when initiating by template switching to the 3' end of the RNA (Mohr et al., 2013; Katibah et al., 2014; Nottingham et al., 2016; Qin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a background claim supported by citations and demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplements 3-5 showing full-length reads of tRNAs and other sncRNAs.

claim: TGIRT-seq profiles human miRNAs with bias equal to or less than alternative methods in size selected RNA preparations.
source: In size selected RNA preparations, TGIRT-seq profiles human miRNAs with bias equal to or less than alternative methods (Mohr et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a background claim about TGIRT-seq performance supported by citations.

claim: In a validation study using rRNA-depleted, chemically fragmented human reference RNAs with External RNA Control Consortium spike-ins, TGIRT-seq gave better quantitation of mRNAs and spike ins, more uniform 5' to 3' coverage of mRNA sequences, detected more splice junctions, particularly near the 5' ends of mRNAs, and had higher strand specificity when compared to benchmark TruSeq-v3 datasets.
source: In a validation study using rRNA-depleted, chemically fragmented human reference RNAs with External RNA Control Consortium spike-ins, TGIRT-seq gave better quantitation of mRNAs and spike ins, more uniform 5' to 3' coverage of mRNA sequences, detected more splice junctions, particularly near the 5' ends of mRNAs, and had higher strand specificity when compared to benchmark TruSeq-v3 datasets (Nottingham et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a background claim about TGIRT-seq performance supported by citation to a previous validation study.

claim: TGIRT-seq enables the simultaneous sequencing of chemically fragmented mRNAs together with tRNAs and other structured sncRNAs, which were poorly represented in TruSeq datasets, even after chemical fragmentation.
source: This study also showed that TGIRT-seq enables the simultaneous sequencing of chemically fragmented mRNAs together with tRNAs and other structured sncRNAs, which were poorly represented in the TruSeq datasets, even after chemical fragmentation (Nottingham et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a background claim about TGIRT-seq capabilities supported by citation.

claim: TGIRT-seq enables simultaneous quantitative profiling of mRNA fragments and sncRNAs of > 60 nt, but under-represents smaller RNAs due in part to differential loss during library clean-up to remove adapter dimers.
source: A subsequent study of chemically fragmented human cellular RNAs with customized spike-ins confirmed these findings and showed that TGIRT-seq enables simultaneous quantitative profiling of mRNA fragments and sncRNAs of > 60 nt, but under-represents smaller RNAs due in part to differential loss during library clean-up to remove adapter dimers (Boivin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a background claim about TGIRT-seq performance and limitations supported by citation.

claim: Recent TGIRT-seq profiling of structured RNAs in unfragmented cellular RNA preparations from human cells revealed previously unannotated sncRNAs, including novel snoRNAs, tRNA-like RNAs, and tRNA fragments (tRFs).
source: Recent TGIRT-seq profiling of structured RNAs in unfragmented cellular RNA preparations from human cells revealed previously unannotated sncRNAs, including novel snoRNAs, tRNA-like RNAs, and tRNA fragments (tRFs) (Boivin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a background claim about previous TGIRT-seq findings supported by citation.

claim: The TGIRT-seq datasets were obtained from commercial human plasma pooled from multiple healthy individuals and prepared by apheresis with EDTA as the anticoagulant.
source: The TGIRT-seq datasets in this study were obtained from commercial human plasma pooled from multiple healthy individuals and prepared by apheresis with EDTA as the anticoagulant (IPLA-N-K2E; Innovative Research).
evidence: This is a methodological claim describing the sample source.

claim: Nucleic acids were extracted from 4 mL of plasma by using a QIAamp ccfDNA/RNA kit and treated with NaOH to obtain RNA-free plasma DNA or with DNase I, exonuclease I (Exo I) or Exo I + DNase I to obtain plasma RNA with minimal residual DNA.
source: For each dataset, nucleic acids were extracted from 4 mL of plasma by using a QIAamp ccfDNA/RNA kit (Qiagen) and treated with NaOH to obtain RNA-free plasma DNA (n = 4) or with DNase I (n = 12), exonuclease I (Exo I; n = 1) or Exo I + DNase I (n = 2) to obtain plasma RNA with minimal residual DNA (referred to collectively as DNase-treated plasma RNA; n = 15).
evidence: This is a methodological claim describing the sample preparation procedure.

claim: Each plasma nucleic acid preparation gave ~10 ng of nucleic acid, which yielded ~8 ng DNA or ~2 ng RNA, as judged by Bioanalyzer analysis.
source: Each preparation gave ~10 ng of nucleic acid, which yielded ~8 ng DNA or ~2 ng RNA, as judged by Bioanalyzer analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the sample preparation supported by Bioanalyzer data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The initial TGIRT-template switching reaction was done at a lower salt concentration (200 instead of 450 mM), which increases the efficiency of 3'-RNA-seq adapter addition.
source: First, the initial TGIRT-template switching reaction was done at a lower salt concentration (200 instead of 450 mM), which increases the efficiency of 3'-RNA-seq adapter addition (Wu and Lambowitz, 2017; Lentzsch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a methodological improvement described with supporting citations.

claim: A modified R2R adapter was used that substantially decreases adapter-dimer formation.
source: Second, we used a modified R2R adapter that substantially decreases adapter-dimer formation (Xu et al., 2019), thereby improving the representation of very small RNAs, such as miRNAs and short tRNA fragments (tRFs).
evidence: This is a methodological improvement described with supporting citation.

claim: A modified R1R adapter with a 6-nt UMI was used to deconvolute duplicate reads.
source: Finally, we used a modified R1R adapter with a 6-nt UMI to deconvolute duplicate reads (Wu and Lambowitz, 2017).
evidence: This is a methodological improvement described with supporting citation.

claim: Mapping rates for the DNase-treated plasma RNA datasets (n = 15) ranged from 82–96%.
source: Mapping rates for the DNase-treated plasma RNA datasets (n = 15) ranged from 82–96% (Supplementary file 1), with pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients r = 0.67–1.00 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the sequencing data analysis.

claim: The read-span distributions for the untreated and NaOH-treated plasma DNA samples showed two broad peaks, one at 130–180 nt, corresponding to plasma DNA protected in chromatosomes or trimmed mononucleosomes, and the other at 50–100 nt corresponding to nicked DNA strands that are protected by transcription factors or other bound proteins.
source: The read-span distributions for the untreated and NaOH-treated plasma DNA samples showed two broad peaks, one at 130–180 nt, corresponding to plasma DNA protected in chromatosomes (nucleosomes plus linker histone) or trimmed mononucleosomes, and the other at 50–100 nt corresponding to nicked DNA strands that are protected by transcription factors or other bound proteins (Figure 1B), in agreement with previous studies (Chandrananda et al., 2015; Snyder et al., 2016; Wu and Lambowitz, 2017).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis shown in Figure 1B and is consistent with previous studies cited.

claim: All of the dsDNA in the untreated plasma nucleic acid sample was sensitive to DNase I.
source: Bioanalyzer traces using a High Sensitivity DNA kit showed that all of the dsDNA in the untreated plasma nucleic acid sample was sensitive to DNase I (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a result from the Bioanalyzer analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The read-span distributions for plasma RNA samples obtained after treatment with DNase I or Exo I ± DNase I showed a broad peak of 40–80 nt.
source: The read-span distributions for plasma RNA samples obtained after treatment with DNase I (n = 12) or Exo I ± DNase I (n = 3) showed a broad peak of 40–80 nt (Figure 1B), which corresponded to a similarly sized peak that was detected and confirmed to be NaOH-sensitive in Bioanalyzer traces obtained by using an RNA 6000 Pico Kit (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: For NaOH-treated plasma DNA samples, most of the plasma DNA read pairs mapped to genomic repeats (46%), unannotated sequences (26%), or protein-coding genes (21%).
source: For NaOH-treated plasma DNA samples (n = 4), the overall distribution of read pairs was similar to that simulated for random sampling of human genomic DNA (WGS-sim; simulated by ART). Most of these plasma DNA read pairs mapped to genomic repeats (46%; Repbase), unannotated sequences (26%), or protein-coding genes (21%; Figure 1C), with the read pairs mapping to protein-coding genes equally distributed between the sense and antisense strands (Figure 1E) and most of the bases in these read pairs located within introns (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The plasma RNA samples after treatment with DNase I gave read pairs mapping to 26,000–43,000 different genes.
source: The plasma RNA samples after treatment with DNase I (n = 12), Exo I ± DNase I (n = 3), or DNase I + T4 polynucleotide kinase to remove 3' phosphates (n = 3) gave read pairs mapping to 26,000–43,000 different genes (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: For the DNase I-treated plasma RNA, high proportions of the read pairs mapped to cellular or mitochondrial (Mt) tRNAs (44% and 29%, respectively) followed by cellular and Mt rRNAs (16% and 5%, respectively), other sncRNAs (4.6%), repeats (0.8%), protein-coding gene transcripts (0.6%), other ncRNAs (0.1%), and miRNAs (0.006%).
source: For the DNase I-treated plasma RNA, high proportions of the read pairs mapped to cellular or mitochondrial (Mt) tRNAs (44% and 29%, respectively) followed by cellular and Mt rRNAs (16% and 5%, respectively), other sncRNAs (4.6%), repeats (Repbase; 0.8%), protein-coding gene transcripts (0.6%), other ncRNAs (0.1%), and miRNAs (0.006%; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Treatment of plasma nucleic acids with T4 polynucleotide kinase to remove 3' phosphates increased the proportions of total reads mapping to 18S and 28S rRNAs (to 33%), repeats (to 9%), and protein-coding genes (to 4.1%).
source: Treatment of plasma nucleic acids with T4 polynucleotide kinase to remove 3' phosphates increased the proportions of total reads mapping to 18S and 28S rRNAs (to 33%), repeats (to 9%), and protein-coding genes (to 4.1%; Figure 1C; lane 6).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis showing the effect of 3'-phosphate removal.

claim: The proportions of protein-coding gene reads mapping to the antisense strand (17–36%) and bases within introns (63–73%) were higher than those in TGIRT-seq datasets of cellular RNAs (10% and 24%, respectively), suggesting that intron and antisense RNAs may be selectively exported or stable in plasma.
source: In agreement with previous findings (Qin et al., 2016), the proportions of protein-coding gene reads mapping to the antisense strand (17–36%; Figure 1E) and bases within introns (63–73%; Figure 1F) were higher than those in TGIRT-seq datasets of cellular RNAs (10% and 24%, respectively [Nottingham et al., 2016]), suggesting that intron and antisense RNAs may be selectively exported or stable in plasma.
evidence: This is a comparative result with an interpretive inference about the biological significance.

claim: The most abundant sncRNAs in the DNase I-treated plasma RNA samples were tRNAs (36,766 CPM for Val-CAC, the most abundant isodecoder species) followed by Y RNAs (15,247 CPM for RNY4, the most abundant species), and 7SL RNA (158–1,504 CPM for the three 7SL RNA genes).
source: The most abundant sncRNAs in the DNase I-treated plasma RNA samples were tRNAs (36,766 counts per million (CPM) for Val-CAC, the most abundant isodecoder species) followed by Y RNAs (15,247 CPM for RNY4, the most abundant species), and 7SL RNA (158–1,504 CPM for the three 7SL RNA genes; Figure 1D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: TGIRT-seq showed that most of the cellular and Mt tRNAs detected in plasma were full-length mature tRNAs, which cannot be fully reverse transcribed by retroviral RTs.
source: As found previously (Qin et al., 2016), TGIRT-seq showed that most of the cellular and Mt tRNAs detected in plasma were full-length mature tRNAs, which cannot be fully reverse transcribed by retroviral RTs (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4, respectively).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4, with comparison to retroviral RT capabilities.

claim: The plasma preparations contained lower concentrations of specific cellular 5'-tRNA halves (0.02–68 CPM), 3'-tRNA halves (0.02–9,036 CPM), and shorter tRNA fragments.
source: The plasma preparations also contained lower concentrations of specific cellular 5'-tRNA halves (0.02–68 CPM), 3'-tRNA halves (0.02–9,036 CPM), and shorter tRNA fragments (5'-tRFs, 0.02–39 CPM; 3'-tRFs, 3–640 CPM; and internal 2-tRFs, 0.02–7 CPM), with the proportion of reads corresponding to some 5'-tRNA halves and 5'-tRFs increasing after 3'-phosphate removal (e.g., 5' half Gly-CCC, 2.9-fold increase; 5'-tRF Cys-GCA, 2-fold increase; see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: TGIRT-seq identified 5' ends of 3'-tRFs that extend beyond the m1A modification site in the TψC loop, which is a strong stop for retroviral RTs and can be mistaken for the 5' end of 3'-tRFs.
source: Notably, TGIRT-seq identified 5' ends of 3'-tRFs that extend beyond the m1A modification site in the TψC loop, which is a strong stop for retroviral RTs and can be mistaken for the 5' end of 3'-tRFs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Kumar et al., 2014; Reinsborough et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3, highlighting an advantage of TGIRT-seq over retroviral RT methods.

claim: Other structured sncRNAs in plasma, including Vault RNAs, snoRNAs, snRNAs, 7SK RNA, 7SL RNA, 5S rRNA and 5.8S rRNA, were present largely as full-length mature transcripts.
source: Other structured sncRNAs in plasma, including Vault RNAs, snoRNAs, snRNAs, 7SK RNA, 7SL RNA, 5S rRNA and 5.8S rRNA, were also present largely as full-length mature transcripts (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), in agreement with previous findings (Qin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The improved TGIRT-seq method detected 263 miRNAs annotated as high confidence miRNAs in miRbase v20 in the DNase I-treated plasma RNAs datasets.
source: The improved TGIRT-seq method detected 263 miRNAs annotated as high confidence miRNAs in miRbase v20 in the DNase I-treated plasma RNAs datasets (n = 12; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: The miRNAs detected by TGIRT-seq were a mixture of pre- and mature miRNA, passenger strands, and longer transcripts, whose proportions varied for different miRNA species.
source: As found previously using TGIRT-seq (Qin et al., 2016), these were a mixture of pre- and mature miRNA, passenger strands, and longer transcripts, whose proportions varied for different miRNA species (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The most abundant miRNA detected by TGIRT-seq, miR-223, was present at only 2.89 CPM, considerably lower than the most abundant similarly sized 3'-tRFs.
source: The most abundant miRNA detected by TGIRT-seq, miR-223, was present at only 2.89 CPM (Figure 1—figure supplement 6), considerably lower than the most abundant similarly sized 3'-tRFs (Glu-TTC, 640 CPM; Glu-CTC, 510 CPM; Lys-CTT, 121 CPM; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from the data analysis.

claim: Only a very low proportion of reads (< 0.001%) mapped to piRNA loci, and none corresponded to a mature piRNA.
source: Only a very low proportion of reads (< 0.001%) mapped to piRNA loci (Figure 1D; lanes 4–6), and none corresponded to a mature piRNA, even though under the lower salt conditions used for library construction TGIRT-III can template switch to and reverse transcribe RNAs with 2'-O-methylated 3' ends characteristic of piRNAs (Lentzsch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis with a note about the technical capability of the method.

claim: Kraken2 identified 2.83 million RNA reads assigned to bacteria, with the most abundant phyla being Proteobacteria, Actinobacteria, and Firmicutes and the most abundant genera being Pseudomonas, Salmonella, Acinetobacter, Halomonas, and Bacillus.
source: Kraken2 assigns reads to bacterial, viral, and archaeal genomes based on matches to unique k-mer sequences in a database of non-redundant bacterial, viral, and archaeal sequences compiled from RefSeq. We thus identified 2.83 million RNA reads assigned to bacteria, with the most abundant phyla being Proteobacteria, Actinobacteria, and Firmicutes and the most abundant genera being Pseudomonas, Salmonella, Acinetobacter, Halomonas, and Bacillus, consistent with other studies (Potgieter et al., 2015; Pan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a result from the metagenomic analysis using Kraken2.

claim: A much smaller number of non-human RNA reads (~52,000) were assigned to viruses, the most abundant being Parvoviridae and Mason-Pfizer monkey virus, a retrovirus.
source: A much smaller number of non-human RNA reads (~52,000) were assigned to viruses, the most abundant being Parvoviridae and Mason-Pfizer monkey virus, a retrovirus (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a result from the metagenomic analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The combined NaOH-treated plasma DNA datasets contained only 12,000 non-human reads, much lower than 1% reported in another study using plasma prepared by a different method.
source: The combined NaOH-treated plasma DNA datasets (n = 4; 46 million deduplicated reads) contained only 12,000 non-human reads, much lower than 1% reported in another study using plasma prepared by a different method (Kowarsky et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the metagenomic analysis with comparison to another study.

claim: Most (93.3%) of the non-human DNA reads were assigned by Kraken2 to bacteria, mainly Pseudomonas spp., with only 64 reads assigned to viruses, mostly human β herpesvirus 6B.
source: Most (93.3%) of the non-human DNA reads were assigned by Kraken2 to bacteria, mainly Pseudomonas spp., with only 64 reads assigned to viruses, mostly human β herpesvirus 6B (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from the metagenomic analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The commercial plasma preparations had been screened by the supplier for hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, HIV-1, HIV-2, and syphilis, and no reads mapping to any of these pathogens were found.
source: The commercial plasma preparations had been screened by the supplier for hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, HIV-1, HIV-2, and syphilis, and we found no reads mapping to any of these pathogens.
evidence: This is a result from the metagenomic analysis confirming the supplier's screening.

claim: A separate search for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) found 28 deduplicated RNA reads and no DNA reads.
source: A separate search for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) found 28 deduplicated RNA reads and no DNA reads.
evidence: This is a result from the metagenomic analysis.

claim: The low levels of viral nucleic acids found could reflect that apheresis-prepared plasma has very low levels of leukocyte and platelet contamination, the presence of which correlates with increased risk of viral and prion disease transmission in plasma used for clinical purposes.
source: More generally, the low levels of viral nucleic acids found here could also reflect that apheresis-prepared plasma has very low levels of leukocyte and platelet contamination, the presence of which correlates with increased risk of viral and prion disease transmission in plasma used for clinical purposes (Valbonesi et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results with supporting citation.

claim: The proportion of the TGIRT-seq reads mapping to protein-coding genes was relatively low (0.6–4.1%), but nevertheless sufficient to identify mRNAs originating from 15,000 to 19,000 different protein-coding genes.
source: In the plasma prepared by apheresis from multiple healthy individuals, the proportion of the TGIRT-seq reads mapping to protein-coding genes was relatively low (0.6–4.1%; Figure 1C, lanes 4–6), but nevertheless sufficient to identify mRNAs originating from 15,000 to 19,000 different protein-coding genes, with the highest number of different mRNAs detected after 3'-phosphate removal with T4 polynucleotide kinase (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis shown in Figures 1C and 3A-B.

claim: The identities and relative abundances of different protein-coding gene transcripts in the apheresis-prepared plasma were broadly similar to those in the previous TGIRT analysis of plasma prepared by Ficoll-cushion sedimentation of blood from a healthy male individual (r = 0.62–0.80).
source: The identities and relative abundances of different protein-coding gene transcripts in the apheresis-prepared plasma were broadly similar to those in the previous TGIRT analysis of plasma prepared by Ficoll-cushion sedimentation of blood from a healthy male individual (Qin et al., 2016) (r = 0.62–0.80; Figure 3C) and between high quality plasma samples similarly prepared from five healthy females in a collaborative study with Dr. Naoto Ueno, M.D. Anderson (r  = 0.53–0.67; manuscript in preparation).
evidence: This is a comparative result shown in Figure 3C with correlation coefficients.

claim: The SMART-Seq libraries mapped to > 16,000 protein-coding genes with a transcript per million value (TPM) > 0.1.
source: The SMART-Seq libraries (n = 4) were then sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 500 to obtain a total of 2.6 million 2 × 75 nt reads that mapped to > 16,000 protein-coding genes with a transcript per million value (TPM) > 0.1.
evidence: This is a result from the SMART-Seq analysis.

claim: Bioanalyzer traces showed that the amplified dsDNAs obtained by SMART-Seq prior to Covaris sonication were substantially shorter than those from the cellular RNA control provided with the kit (peaks at 100–200 and 400–700 bp for plasma RNA compared to 700–7,000 bp for the cellular control RNA), indicating that the poly(A)-containing mRNAs detected in plasma by SMART-Seq are enriched in 3' fragments.
source: Bioanalyzer traces showed that the amplified dsDNAs obtained by SMART-Seq prior to Covaris sonication were substantially shorter than those from the cellular RNA control provided with the kit (peaks at 100–200 and 400–700 bp for plasma RNA compared to 700–7,000 bp for the cellular control RNA; Figure 3D), indicating that the poly(A)-containing mRNAs detected in plasma by SMART-Seq are enriched in 3' fragments.
evidence: This is a result from the Bioanalyzer analysis shown in Figure 3D with an interpretation.

claim: Most of the polyadenylated mRNAs detected in DNase I-treated plasma RNA by ultra low input SMART-Seq were also detected by TGIRT-seq at similar TPM values when normalized for protein-coding gene reads (r = 0.61).
source: A scatter plot comparing the relative abundance of transcripts originating from different genes showed that most of the polyadenylated mRNAs detected in DNase I-treated plasma RNA by ultra low input SMART-Seq were also detected by TGIRT-seq at similar TPM values when normalized for protein-coding gene reads (r = 0.61), but with some, mostly lower abundance mRNAs undetected either by TGIRT-seq or SMART-Seq, and with SMART-Seq unable to detect non-polyadenylated histone mRNAs, which are relatively abundant in plasma (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a comparative result shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Heat maps comparing protein-coding gene transcripts detected by TGIRT-seq and SMART-Seq to primary tissue and platelet transcriptome data indicated that the detected mRNA originated largely from hematopoietic tissues, including bone marrow, lymph nodes, and spleen, with contributions from erythrocytes, white blood cells, and platelets.
source: Heat maps comparing protein-coding gene transcripts detected by TGIRT-seq and SMART-Seq to primary tissue and platelet transcriptome data (Schubert et al., 2014; Uhlén et al., 2015; Campbell et al., 2018) indicated that the detected mRNA originated largely from hematopoietic tissues, including bone marrow, lymph nodes, and spleen, with contributions from erythrocytes, white blood cells, and platelets (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D), in agreement with other studies (Koh et al., 2014; Giraldez et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a result from the tissue-of-origin analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: Plots of normalized coverage over all detected mRNAs showed that SMART-Seq under-represented 5'-RNA sequences and over-represented 3'-RNA sequences, as expected for 3'-mRNA fragments, while TGIRT-seq coverage was relatively uniform across most of the length of the detected mRNAs.
source: Plots of normalized coverage over all detected mRNAs showed that SMART-Seq under-represented 5'-RNA sequences and over-represented 3'-RNA sequences, as expected for 3'-mRNA fragments, while TGIRT-seq coverage, with or without 3'-phosphate removal or with chemical fragmentation followed by 3' phosphate removal, was relatively uniform across most of the length of the detected mRNAs (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a comparative result shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Although 3'-phosphate removal increased both the proportion of reads mapping to protein-coding genes and the number of mRNAs detected by TGIRT-seq, neither the 5'- to 3'-coverage nor the abundance of most protein-coding transcripts detected in plasma by TGIRT-seq was strongly affected (r = 0.93 and 0.84, respectively).
source: Notably, although 3'-phosphate removal increased both the proportion of reads mapping to protein-coding genes and the number of mRNAs detected by TGIRT-seq (see above), neither the 5'- to 3'-coverage nor the abundance of most protein-coding transcripts detected in plasma by TGIRT-seq was strongly affected (Figure 3A,B and F; r = 0.93 and 0.84, respectively).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis shown in Figure 3A, B, and F.

claim: Only a small proportion of protein-coding gene transcripts increased significantly after 3'-phosphate removal (0.41% by differential expression analysis using DESeq2; adjusted p-value < 0.01).
source: This reflects that many of the additional protein-coding gene transcripts detected after 3'-phosphate removal had relatively low read counts and that the abundance of only a small proportion of protein-coding gene transcripts increased significantly after this treatment (0.41% by differential expression analysis using DESeq2; adjusted p-value < 0.01).
evidence: This is a result from differential expression analysis.

claim: These findings are consistent with the suggestion that many mRNA fragments in plasma have 3' OH termini, as expected for RNA fragments generated by cellular ribonucleases that function in mRNA processing or turnover.
source: Because 3' phosphates inhibit RNA-seq adapter addition by TGIRT template switching (Mohr et al., 2013), these findings are consistent with the suggestion from the previous TGIRT-seq analysis (Qin et al., 2016) that many mRNA fragments in plasma have 3' OH termini, as expected for RNA fragments generated by cellular ribonucleases that function in mRNA processing or turnover (Houseley and Tollervey, 2009; Schoenberg and Maquat, 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results with supporting citations.

claim: Peak calling using a read coverage cutoff of ≥ 5, a false discovery rate cutoff of 0.05, and a requirement that the peak was detected in at least 5 of the 15 samples yielded 1,036 peaks that were enriched in the DNase-treated plasma RNA over the base line control.
source: Peak calling using a read coverage cutoff of ≥ 5, a false discovery rate cutoff of 0.05 (q-value assigned by MACS2), and a requirement that the peak was detected in at least 5 of the 15 samples to avoid batch effects yielded 1,036 peaks that were enriched in the DNase-treated plasma RNA over the base line control.
evidence: This is a result from the peak calling analysis.

claim: After filtering, 950 high confidence peaks ranging in size from 59 to 1,207 nt with ≥ 5 high quality read alignments at the peak maximum were identified.
source: After further filtering to remove read alignments with MAPQ < 30 (a cutoff that eliminates reads mapping equally well at more than one locus) or ≥ 5 mismatches from the mapped locus, we were left with 950 high confidence peaks ranging in size from 59 to 1,207 nt with ≥ 5 high quality read alignments at the peak maximum (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from the peak calling analysis.

claim: About half of the peaks (467 peaks; 50.7%) contained or overlapped an ENCODE eCLIP annotated RBP-binding site in a long RNA.
source: About half of the peaks (467 peaks; 50.7%) contained or overlapped an ENCODE eCLIP annotated RBP-binding site in a long RNA (i.e., a mRNA, lncRNA, or pseudogene RNA).
evidence: This is a result from the peak annotation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The 467 peaks with an ENCODE eCLIP annotated RBP-binding site contained or overlapped the binding sites for 90 of the 109 RBPs searched initially in the eCLIP datasets, including 75 that had been shown previously to be part of the plasma proteome.
source: The 467 peaks with an ENCODE eCLIP annotated RBP-binding site contained or overlapped the binding sites for 90 of the 109 RBPs searched initially in the eCLIP datasets, including 75 that had been shown previously to be part of the plasma proteome (Nanjappa et al., 2014; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from the peak annotation analysis with reference to the plasma proteome.

claim: Simulations using 1,000 sets of 950 peaks with the same size distribution as the 950 called peaks randomly generated from the sequences of the genes encoding long RNAs detected in plasma indicated that the enrichment of RBP-binding site sequences in the 467 identified peaks was statistically significant (p < 0.001).
source: Simulations using 1,000 sets of 950 peaks with the same size distribution as the 950 called peaks randomly generated from the sequences of the genes encoding long RNAs detected in plasma indicated that the enrichment of RBP-binding site sequences in the 467 identified peaks was statistically significant (p < 0.001; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a result from statistical simulation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The six RBPs with the most prevalent binding sites in plasma RNAs based on the number of assigned peaks included: three DEAD-box RNA helicases (DDX3X, DDX6, and DDX55); YBX3; LARP4; and EFTUD2.
source: The six RBPs with the most prevalent binding sites in plasma RNAs based on the number of assigned peaks included: three DEAD-box RNA helicases, DDX3X (Figure 5A), DDX6, and DDX55; YBX3, a homologue of the low specificity RBP YBX1, which is not included in the ENCODE eCLIP datasets but of interest because it binds 5' TOP mRNAs and functions in sorting sncRNAs into exosomes (Figure 5B; Evdokimova et al., 2001; Shurtleff et al., 2017; (iii) LARP4, a protein that regulates translation Figure 5C); (iv) and EFTUD2, an RNA splicing factor (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a result from the RBP-binding site analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 5.

claim: Seven of the top 15 RBPs with the most prevalent binding sites in plasma (DDX3X, DDX6, DHX30, LARP4, SERBP1, SND1, and YBX3) are components of stress granules.
source: Notably, seven of these top 15 proteins (DDX3X, DDX6, DHX30, LARP4, SERBP1, SND1, and YBX3) are components of stress granules (Markmiller et al., 2018; Nunes et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a result from the RBP-binding site analysis with reference to stress granule composition.

claim: Twenty-nine peaks identified as containing RBP-binding sites were full-length excised intron RNAs.
source: While most of the potential RBP-binding sites identified by peak calling against the human genome reference sequence corresponded to fragments of mRNA exons (409 binding sites), pseudogenes transcripts (10 binding sites), or annotated antisense RNAs (two binding sites), 46 mapped to introns, and surprisingly, 29 corresponded to short, putatively structured, full-length excised intron RNAs (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from the peak annotation analysis.

claim: Peak calling against the human transcriptome reference sequence identified 806 high confidence peaks, the large majority of which (638 peaks, 79%) were identical or overlapped the 467 RBP-binding site peaks identified by mapping to the human genome reference sequence.
source: To address this possibility, we mapped the reads in the combined DNase-treated datasets (n = 15) to a human transcriptome reference sequence (Ensemble human cDNA references) and obtained ~0.26 million deduplicated read pairs that were used as input for MACS2 without a control dataset (Zhang et al., 2008). Using the same peak-calling and filtering parameters as above, we identified 806 high confidence peaks (denoted by peak IDs beginning with T), the large majority of which (638 peaks, 79%) were identical or overlapped the 467 RBP-binding site peaks identified by mapping to the human genome reference sequence.
evidence: This is a result from the transcriptome-based peak calling analysis.

claim: Of the 168 newly identified peaks from transcriptome mapping, 135 overlapped annotated binding sites for 57 RBPs, only five of which were not identified by peak calling against the genome sequence (AKAP8L, FXR1, RBFOX2, SMNDC1, and TARDBP).
source: Of the 168 newly identified peaks, 135 (80 in mRNAs, 15 in pseudogenes, 11 in antisense RNAs, eight in lincRNAs, and 21 in other lncRNAs) overlapped annotated binding sites for 57 RBPs, only five of which were not identified by peak calling against the genome sequence (AKAP8L, FXR1, RBFOX2, SMNDC1, and TARDBP; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from the transcriptome-based peak calling analysis.

claim: Scatter plots showed that the relative abundances of the different RBP-binding sites in plasma RNAs differed markedly from those in the ENCODE eCLIP cellular RNA datasets.
source: As expected for different populations of mRNAs in plasma and cells, scatter plots showed that the relative abundances of the different RBP-binding sites in plasma RNAs differed markedly from those in the ENCODE eCLIP cellular RNA datasets (without or with the inclusion of peaks mapping to the human transcriptome and both for the original annotation for 109 different RBPs and annotation with irreproducible discovery rate (IDR) analysis from the ENCODE website for 150 different RBPs; Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a comparative result shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Plasma RNAs are particularly enriched in binding sites for stress granule proteins (including DDX3X, DDX6, DHX30, LARP4, IGF2BP3, PABPC4, PCBP1, RPS3, SERBP1, SND1, and YBX3).
source: Notably, stress granule proteins (bold letters) comprised a high proportion of the RBPs whose binding sites were enriched in plasma RNAs, consistent with a previously suggested link between RNP granules, EV packaging, and RNA export (Shurtleff et al., 2017; Temoche-Diaz et al., 2019) (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a result from the comparative analysis with an interpretation linking to previous findings.

claim: Two hundred and thirteen peaks that mapped to exons or pseudogenes in the human genome reference sequence did not correspond to ENCODE eCLIP-annotated RBP-binding sites or genomic repeats.
source: Two hundred and thirteen peaks that mapped to exons or pseudogenes in the human genome reference sequence did not correspond to ENCODE eCLIP-annotated RBP-binding sites or genomic repeats, and an additional 33 such peaks were identified by mapping to the human transcriptome (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplements 1–3, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from the peak annotation analysis.

claim: Twenty five of the 246 exon and pseudogene peaks without RBP-binding sites or repeat annotations were classified by Infernal/Rfam analysis into four types of known RNA structures: 21 histone 3'-UTR stem-loops, an iron response element (IRE I), a selenocysteine insertion sequence 1, and two potential pre-miRNA stem-loop structures.
source: Twenty five of these 246 peaks were classified by Infernal/Rfam analysis (Kalvari et al., 2018) into four types of known RNA structures: 21 histone 3'-UTR stem-loops required for 3'-end processing of histone mRNAs; an iron response element (IRE I) in a ferritin light chain (FTL) exon; a selenocysteine insertion sequence 1, which directs the translation of UGA as SelCys; and two potential pre-miRNA stem-loop structures, with the closest match for both being mouse miR-692, which has no annotated human homolog (Figure 7 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from the RNA structure analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Of the 221 exon and pseudogene peaks without known RNA structure classifications, 213 could be folded by RNAfold into stable RNA secondary structures with a calculated minimum free energy (MFE; ΔG) ≤ −12 kcal/mol.
source: To evaluate whether these peaks contained RNAs that could potentially fold into stable secondary structures, we used RNAfold, a tool that is widely used for this purpose with the understanding that the predicted structures remain to be validated and could differ under physiological conditions or due to interactions with proteins. Of the 221 exon and pseudogene peaks, 213 could be folded by RNAfold into stable RNA secondary structures with a calculated minimum free energy (MFE; ΔG) ≤ −12 kcal/mol (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from the RNA secondary structure prediction analysis.

claim: Simulations using peaks randomly generated from long RNA gene sequences indicated that enrichment of RNAs with more stable secondary structures (lower MFEs) in the called RNA peaks was statistically significant (p ≤ 0.019).
source: Subject to the caveats above regarding conclusions drawn from RNAfold, simulations using peaks randomly generated from long RNA gene sequences indicated that enrichment of RNAs with more stable secondary structures (lower MFEs) in the called RNA peaks was statistically significant (p ≤ 0.019; Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a result from statistical simulation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Although Repbase-annotated sequence repeats constituted only 0.8–2.1% of the reads in the DNase-treated plasma RNA datasets, they comprised almost a quarter of the RNA peaks identified by peak calling (213 peaks; 23.1%).
source: Although Repbase-annotated sequence repeats constituted only 0.8–2.1% of the reads in the DNase-treated plasma RNA datasets (Figure 1C), they comprised almost a quarter of the RNA peaks identified by peak calling (213 peaks; 23.1%), including 154 comprised of or containing short tandem repeats (also referred to as simple repeats or microsatellite sequences) and 59 corresponding to transposable element RNAs (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from the peak annotation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The peaks for the short tandem repeat RNAs in human plasma had a surprisingly narrow length distribution (sharp peak ~80 nt) with > 50% having complete or nearly complete read coverage across the annotated repeat region.
source: The peaks for the short tandem repeat RNAs in human plasma had a surprisingly narrow length distribution (sharp peak ~80 nt) with > 50% having complete or nearly complete read coverage across the annotated repeat region (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is a result from the repeat RNA analysis shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: Of the top 15 Repbase-annotated repeat types with the highest peak count, 11 were low complexity sequences, such as polypurine or polypyrimidine tracts or simple repeat RNAs, and four were transposable element RNAs.
source: Of the top 15 Repbase-annotated repeat types with the highest peak count, 11 were low complexity sequences, such as polypurine or polypyrimidine tracts or simple repeat RNAs (e.g., (CCG)n and (TTC)n), and four were transposable element RNAs (AluSx, AluJb, FLAM_C and LINE-1 element HAL1-3A_ME) (Figure 4D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from the repeat RNA analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: An Empirical Bayes method identified the top 15 repeat sequences with the largest differences in the percentage of sense (+) orientation reads between DNase-treated plasma RNA and NaOH-treated plasma DNA, and all corresponded to tandem repeats of short (3–6 nt) sequences, including centromeric and telomeric repeats.
source: To address this issue, we used an Empirical Bayes method (Materials and methods and Figure 8C) to identify the top 15 repeat sequences with the largest differences in the percentage of sense (+) orientation reads between DNase-treated plasma RNA and NaOH-treated plasma DNA and found that all corresponded to tandem repeats of short (3–6 nt) sequences, including centromeric and telomeric repeats (Figure 4E, Figure 8D, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is a result from the strand-specificity analysis shown in Figure 4E and Figure 8D.

claim: Differential expression analysis for transposable element RNAs found that those with highest enrichments in plasma RNA compared to plasma DNA included endogenous retroviral, LINE-1, and Alu RNAs.
source: Differential expression analysis for transposable element RNAs found that those with highest enrichments in plasma RNA compared to plasma DNA included endogenous retroviral, LINE-1, and Alu RNAs (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is a result from the differential expression analysis shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Peak calling identified 44 different introns for which full-length excised intron RNAs were detected in plasma (counting seven peaks corresponding to the same intron in PKD1 and six pseudogenes as a single intron).
source: Twenty-nine peaks identified as containing RBP-binding sites were full-length excised intron RNAs. An additional 14 such peaks were found among those mapping to long RNAs but not containing an annotated RBP-binding site, and another seven (denoted by IDs beginning with M) were not called as peaks but were identified as containing annotated miRNAs sequences. As discussed further below, seven of these 50 intron peaks corresponded to the same intron found in the PKD1 gene and six of its pseudogenes. Counting these seven peaks as a single intron, we identified 44 different introns for which full-length excised intron RNAs were detected in plasma.
evidence: This is a result from the intron RNA analysis.

claim: All of the full-length excised intron RNAs detected in plasma corresponded to short introns with lengths 73–210 nt.
source: All of the full-length excised intron RNAs detected in plasma corresponded to short introns with lengths 73–210 nt (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from the intron RNA analysis.

claim: All full-length excised intron RNAs were identified by at least five deduplicated TGIRT-seq reads containing the complete intron sequence beginning with a 5' GU and ending with a 3' AG and could be folded by RNAfold into a stem-loop structures with a minimum free energy (MFE; ΔG ≤ −18.7 kcal/mol).
source: All were identified by at least five deduplicated TGIRT-seq reads containing the complete intron sequence beginning with a 5' GU and ending with a 3' AG and could be folded by RNAfold into a stem-loop structures with a minimum free energy (MFE; ΔG ≤ −18.7 kcal/mol) (examples shown in Figure 9A–F).
evidence: This is a result from the intron RNA analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: The full-length excised intron RNAs are likely linear molecules, as the TGIRT-seq reads begin precisely at the 5' GU and end precisely at the 3' AG with no indication of mismatches or impediments that might be indicative of read through of a branch point in a lariat RNA.
source: These intron RNAs are likely linear molecules, as the TGIRT-seq reads begin precisely at the 5' GU and end precisely at the 3' AG with no indication of mismatches or impediments that might be indicative of read through of a branch point in a lariat RNA.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the sequencing data.

claim: In several cases, the reads corresponding to full-length excised intron RNAs had one or two non-templated U or A residues at their 3' end, reminiscent of non-templated 3' A-tails found for yeast linear introns that accumulate in stationary phase cells.
source: In several cases, the reads corresponding to full-length excised intron RNAs had one or two non-templated U or A residues at their 3' end, reminiscent of non-templated 3' A-tails found for yeast linear introns that accumulate in stationary phase cells (Morgan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a result from the sequencing data analysis with comparison to yeast findings.

claim: Thirteen of the full-length excised intron RNAs detected in plasma, including the most abundant, DOCK6 intron 25, corresponded to annotated agotrons.
source: Thirteen of the full-length excised intron RNAs that we detected in plasma, including the most abundant, DOCK6 intron 25 (ID#468, 389 deduplicated reads, 7 CPM), corresponded to annotated agotrons, intron RNAs that were identified as binding to Argonaute-2 protein (AGO2) in HITS-CLIP-seq datasets and shown to repress mRNA translation in reporter assays (Hansen et al., 2016; Hansen, 2018; Figure 4F, Figure 9A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from the intron RNA annotation analysis shown in Figure 4F and Figure 9A.

claim: Ten of the excised intron RNAs detected in plasma corresponded to annotated mirtrons, miRNAs that are processed by DICER from debranched structured intron RNAs.
source: Ten of the excised intron RNAs that we detected in plasma corresponded to annotated mirtrons, miRNAs that are processed by DICER from debranched structured intron RNAs (examples shown in Figure 9B and C; Berezikov et al., 2007; Okamura et al., 2007; Ruby et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a result from the intron RNA annotation analysis shown in Figure 9B and C.

claim: Seven of the ten mirtron pre-miRNAs detected in plasma were also annotated as agotrons.
source: Seven of these ten mirtron pre-miRNAs were also annotated as agotrons (including four of the top 15; green with asterisk in Figure 4F and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from the intron RNA annotation analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: All of the mirtron RNA peaks detected in plasma corresponded to the full-length excised intron RNAs (i.e., the putative pre-miRNA), and none corresponded to the annotated mature miRNA.
source: All of the mirtron RNA peaks detected in plasma corresponded to the full-length excised intron RNAs (i.e., the putative pre-miRNA), to our knowledge the first time such intron-derived pre-miRNAs have been sequenced, and none corresponded to the annotated mature miRNA.
evidence: This is a result from the intron RNA analysis with a claim about novelty.

claim: The remaining 21 putatively structured full-length excised intron RNAs (48% of the total detected in plasma) did not correspond to an identified agotron or mirtron.
source: Significantly, the remaining 21 putatively structured full-length excised intron RNAs, 48% of the total that we detected in plasma, including the second most abundant, PKD1 intron 29 (ID#333; denoted PKD1 in Figure 4F), did not correspond to an identified agotron or mirtron (Supplementary File; additional examples in Figure 9E and F).
evidence: This is a result from the intron RNA annotation analysis shown in Figure 4F and Figure 9E-F.

claim: The reads mapping to PKD1 intron 29 were distributed between the PKD1 gene and the same intron in six PKD1 pseudogenes (PKD1P1-P6), which are located on a distant duplicated segment of the same chromosome.
source: In initial mapping, the reads mapping to PKD1 intron 29 were distributed between the PKD1 gene and the same intron in six PKD1 pseudogenes (PKD1P1-P6), which are located on a distant duplicated segment of the same chromosome (chromosome 16).
evidence: This is a result from the mapping analysis.

claim: The introns in the PKD1 parent gene and all six pseudogenes differed by only a single nucleotide at a known SNP position and were more conserved than the flanking PKD1 exons (6–8 mismatches in the 211 bp 5' exon and 1–3 mismatches in the 127 bp 3' exon), possibly reflecting that this intron has a critical sequence-dependent function.
source: Notably, the introns in the parent and all six pseudogenes differed by only a single nucleotide at a known SNP position and were more conserved than the flanking PKD1 exons (6–8 mismatches in the 211 bp 5' exon and 1–3 mismatches in the 127 bp 3' exon), possibly reflecting that this intron has a critical sequence-dependent function.
evidence: This is a result from the sequence conservation analysis with an interpretive inference.

claim: Only one of the full-length excised introns, PKD1 intron 45 (encoding miR-1225), was conserved in sequence across vertebrates and only six were conserved in sequence across primates (phastCons scores ≥ 0.5).
source: Nevertheless, only one of the full-length excised introns, PKD1 intron 45 (ID# M1; encoding miR-1225), was conserved in sequence across vertebrates and only six were conserved in sequence across primates (phastCons scores ≥ 0.5; Figure 10).
evidence: This is a result from the sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 10.

claim: Sixteen peaks identified as corresponding to annotated RBP-binding sites mapped within introns, and another 15 such peaks were found among those mapping to long RNAs but lacking an annotated RBP-binding site.
source: Sixteen peaks identified as corresponding to annotated RBP-binding sites mapped within introns (see above), and an another 15 such peaks were found among those mapping to long RNAs but lacking an annotated RBP-binding site.
evidence: This is a result from the peak annotation analysis.

claim: Most of the intron peaks (25 peaks, 81%) could be folded by RNAfold into a secondary structure with ΔG ≤ −14.6 kcal/mol.
source: Paralleling findings for mRNA fragments in plasma, most of these intron peaks (25 peaks, 81%) could be folded by RNAfold into a secondary structure with ΔG ≤ −14.6 kcal/mol (examples shown in Figure 11A–E and the remainder in Figure 11—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is a result from the RNA secondary structure prediction analysis shown in Figure 11.

claim: The remaining nine peaks (71–295 nt) mapping to internal segments of intron RNAs were part of retrotransposed mRNAs sequences (432–1,745 nt) that had integrated into seven different long introns (8 to 138 kb).
source: Finally, we found that the remaining nine peaks (71–295 nt) mapping to internal segments of intron RNAs were part of retrotransposed mRNAs sequences (432–1,745 nt) that had integrated into seven different long introns (8 to 138 kb; Figure 11H and I, Figure 12, Figure 12—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the intron RNA analysis shown in Figure 11H-I and Figure 12.

claim: The retrotransposed mRNA sequences originated from six different highly expressed mRNAs (ribosomal protein mRNAs RPS3, RPL18A, and RPL41; translation elongation factor mRNAs EEF1A1 and EEF1G; and β-actin (ACTB) mRNA).
source: These retrotransposed mRNA sequences were identified by a BLAT search for > 95% identity to the called peak in the human genome reference sequence and originated from six different highly expressed mRNAs (ribosomal protein mRNAs RPS3, RPL18A, and RPL41; translation elongation factor mRNAs EEF1A1 and EEF1G; and β-actin (ACTB) mRNA).
evidence: This is a result from the sequence analysis of retrotransposed mRNAs.

claim: All of the retrotransposed mRNA sequences had a short poly(A) tail (9–22 nt) and were flanked by short direct repeat target site duplications (TSDs), hallmarks of LINE-1 RT-mediated retrotransposition.
source: All of these retrotransposed mRNA sequences had a short poly(A) tail (9–22 nt) and were flanked by short direct repeat target site duplications (TSDs; Figure 12, Figure 12—figure supplement 1), hallmarks of LINE-1 RT-mediated retrotransposition (Richardson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a result from the sequence analysis with reference to LINE-1 retrotransposition characteristics.

claim: In all cases, the RNA peak identified in plasma corresponded to a smaller segment of the retrotransposed mRNA sequence that could be folded by RNAfold into a stable RNA secondary structure (ΔG ≤ −16.4 kcal/mole).
source: In all cases, the RNA peak identified in plasma corresponded to a smaller segment of the retrotransposed mRNA sequence that could be folded by RNAfold into a stable RNA secondary structure (ΔG ≤ −16.4 kcal/mole; Figure 11H and I, Figure 11—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a result from the RNA secondary structure prediction analysis shown in Figure 11H-I.

claim: Comparison of genomic sequences showed the retrotransposition events that inserted the mRNA sequences within the introns were relatively recent, with six occurring in primates and two in placental mammals.
source: Comparison of genomic sequences showed the retrotransposition events that inserted the mRNA sequences within the introns were relatively recent, with six occurring in primates and two in placental mammals (Figure 12A and Figure 12—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the comparative genomic analysis shown in Figure 12A and Figure 12—figure supplement 1.

claim: Analysis of two introns with the largest number of homologous genomic sequences across primates and placental mammals showed that both the retrotransposed mRNA sequence and called peak region were more conserved than the flanking intron sequences, consistent with functional importance.
source: Analysis of two introns with the largest number of homologous genomic sequences across primates and placental mammals showed that both the retrotransposed mRNA sequence and called peak region were more conserved than the flanking intron sequences, consistent with functional importance (Figure 12B).
evidence: This is a result from the sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 12B with an interpretive inference.

claim: Only three of the peaks identified by peak calling mapped to unannotated genomic loci.
source: Only three of the peaks identified by peak calling mapped to unannotated genomic loci (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a result from the peak annotation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Twenty-five peaks were identified as antisense transcripts of annotated genomic features.
source: Finally, 25 peaks were identified as antisense transcripts of annotated genomic features (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a result from the peak annotation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Among the 17 antisense peaks mapping to mRNAs or pseudogenes, 12 mapped to hemoglobin genes, four to other highly represented genes (RPS29, TMSB4X, INPP5E, and FTL), and one to a pseudogene.
source: Among the 17 other antisense peaks mapping to mRNAs or pseudogenes, 12 mapped to hemoglobin genes (HBA2, HBA1, HBQ1, HBB, etc.), four to other highly represented genes (RPS29, TMSB4X, INPP5E, and FTL), and one to a pseudogene (Figure 13E–H and Figure 13—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from the antisense peak annotation analysis shown in Figure 13.

claim: Some antisense peaks included antisense reads that extended across two or more spliced exons and/or were mirrored by a partially overlapping antisense DNA peak, suggesting that they contain DNA fragments that are partially protected from DNase I-digestion in an RNA/DNA duplex.
source: While many of these peaks may correspond to bona fide antisense transcripts, some included antisense reads that extended across two or more spliced exons (horizontal orange boxes) and/or were mirrored by a partially overlapping antisense DNA peak (red boxes extending vertically across the coverage tracks and read alignments; Figure 13F–H and Figure 13—figure supplement 1), the latter suggesting that they contain DNA fragments that are partially protected from DNase I-digestion in an RNA/DNA duplex.
evidence: This is a result from the antisense peak analysis shown in Figure 13F-H with an interpretive inference.

claim: Such RNA/DNA duplexes could be remnants of R-loops formed during transcription or cDNAs generated by reverse transcription of a spliced mRNA by an endogenous cellular RT.
source: Such RNA/DNA duplexes could be remnants of R-loops formed during transcription (Sanz et al., 2016) or cDNAs generated by reverse transcription of a spliced mRNA by an endogenous cellular RT.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the antisense peak findings with citation.
